h.select_rule: Discard any hypothesis whose condition is the edited field's own current value, or whose condition merely disables or disconnects the edited component. From the rest, keep 10 with distinct mechanisms and field pairs, favouring those where an informed expert could plausibly bet on either direction.
h.strategy: Two patterns are banned because experts find them obvious: (1) conditioning on the current value of the same field being edited, which just restates that upgrading a weak setting helps more than upgrading a strong one; (2) conditions that make the edited component unused, unreachable or inert. Instead, each hypothesis must link two DIFFERENT fields that interact through a non-trivial mechanism, such as substitution between parallel routes, a capacity already supplied elsewhere, one part acting as a bottleneck for another, or interference that turns a usually helpful edit harmful. No condition setting may appear in more than two hypotheses. Use the gaps and negated assumptions as the source of each idea. In each 'why', name the mechanism and explain why the opposite direction is also a priori plausible.

hyps.why: sklearn scales the L2 term by alpha/batch_size per step, so at tiny batches raising alpha inflates an already large effective penalty and drives underfitting far more than at large batches.
Shrinkage of every layer compounds multiplicatively through three layers and attenuates the forward signal, so extra alpha damages deep nets more.
Because Adam's per-weight step is width-independent, wider nets change their function faster at tiny LRs and so get further toward a good fit within the fixed 243 epochs.
Narrow layers act as information bottlenecks and lose a larger fraction of units to dead ReLUs, so stacking another narrow layer hurts more than adding a wide one.
Update-induced perturbations compound across layers, so an extra layer at already-aggressive LRs makes Adam training more likely to destabilize.
Tiny batches already take many noisy steps per epoch, so a larger step amplifies noise and overshoots, while large-batch runs are step-limited and benefit from a bigger LR.
Wide layers sum many coordinated Adam updates so the per-step function change grows with width, making a higher LR overshoot sooner.
At tiny LRs the number of optimizer steps is the bottleneck, so cutting steps with a larger batch causes underfitting that does not occur when LR is adequate.
Because sklearn's effective L2 strength is alpha/batch_size, enlarging the batch directly relieves over-regularization when alpha is large.
Narrowing a three-layer net tightens several stacked bottlenecks at once, so lost capacity and dead-unit risk compound compared with a single hidden layer.
